title: Small physician practices repeatedly submit the same provider data to many payers for directories and credentialing

history.reason: Signal from a CAQH white paper (interested party) and CMS directory reviews.
Primary documents read: survey-based cost estimate, CMS accuracy review, CMS enrollment burden notice. Evidence is dated (2016-2019) and partly vendor-sourced.

description: Physician practices contract with about 20 health plans on average and must answer separate directory verification and credentialing requests from each, via fax, email, portals and phone. A 2019 industry survey estimates this costs the average practice about $1,000 per month, and CMS reviews found nearly half of Medicare Advantage directory locations contained errors.
customer_segment: Small physician practices (fewer than 5 providers average 13.5 plan contracts and about $319 per month directory cost per the survey); practice managers and credentialing staff. Practice counts not established here.
context: Evidence is from 2016-2019 plus a 2026 federal enrollment notice. Since then federal and state directory rules and CAQH/DataSpring tooling have evolved; current burden is not established. Not about prior authorization.

evidence.text: A September 2019 survey of 1,240 practices found an average of 20.2 health plan contracts per practice (13.5 for practices with fewer than 5 providers).
The same publisher estimates directory maintenance costs the average practice $998.84 per month ($319.46 for practices under 5 providers) and $2.76 billion per year nationally.
CMS found 48.74% of Medicare Advantage directory locations reviewed in round 3 (2017-2018) had at least one inaccuracy, with per-plan rates from 4.63% to 93.02%.
CMS estimates 813,975 CMS-855I Medicare enrollment responses and 1,364,716 annual hours, roughly 1.7 hours each by simple division.
Multiple uncoordinated channels per practice (fax, email, portals) may both consume staff time and cause inconsistent answers, contributing to directory errors.

alternatives: Existing shared platforms (CAQH/DataSpring Provider Data Portal), credentialing outsourcers and enrollment services, and payer-side data mining: coverage, price and adoption by small practices not investigated.
Federal National Directory of Healthcare Providers & Services concept (CMS RFI, 2022): status not verified.

contradictory_evidence.text: The cost and savings figures come from CAQH, which operates and sells a single-platform provider data service; the savings estimate is a projection assuming similar efficiencies, not a measured result.
The CMS reviews measure plan directory accuracy, not practice time, and CMS attributes responsibility mainly to plans; they do not show practice-side burden causes the errors.
The survey is from 2019 and the CMS reviews from 2016-2018; the 2023-2024 CAQH Index reports contain no credentialing or directory cost figures, so current burden is unverified.
The CMS-855I notice implies about 1.7 hours per enrollment application, a modest per-response burden and not a directory estimate.

uncertainty: Unknown: current time and cost per practice, share of practices already using CAQH/shared platforms, effect of the No Surprises Act and state directory laws, whether small practices outsource this, and who pays.
open_questions: What do small practices (under 5 providers) actually spend today on credentialing re-attestation and directory updates, measured independently of CAQH?
How many of the roughly 20 payers accept a shared platform versus requiring separate portals or fax?
How have 2021+ directory verification rules changed practice workload?
next_actions: Find independent (AMA, MGMA, state medical society) surveys or recent government notices quantifying directory and credentialing time.
Read the CAQH/DataSpring directory and credentialing pages and pricing to map existing solutions.
Read the CMS-855I supporting statement for per-response burden assumptions.
